figures.caption: Every distance at once. The darkest entries (orange) are the diameter, 4. The right-hand column is each person's eccentricity: their distance to whoever is farthest. The mean of the 90 off-diagonal entries is 1.978.
figures.alt: A ten by ten table of distances between the ten friends. The diagonal is zero, and every entry is between 1 and 4. The entries equal to 4 are shaded orange and sit in the rows and columns of Jo and of Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev and Eli. A right-hand column lists each person's largest distance.

figures.caption: Repeated search. One breadth-first search from each person gives one row of the table. Five people, five searches, five rows.
figures.alt: Five small copies of the five-person network. In each, a different person is the starting point and every dot shows its distance from that person. Below, a five by five table whose rows are colored to match the five searches that produced them.

figures.caption: The one move that Floyd-Warshall repeats. For a pair of people and one allowed stopover, keep whichever is shorter: the best known ride, or the two rides joined at the stopover.
figures.alt: Three dots in a triangle: Ana at the left, Ben at the right and Cleo above between them. A gray line from Ana to Ben is labeled 9 minutes. Two orange lines, Ana to Cleo at 2 minutes and Cleo to Ben at 3 minutes, are the detour. The text says 2 plus 3 is 5, which beats 9.

figures.caption: Floyd-Warshall on five places and travel minutes. Each step allows one more person as a stopover and rewrites any cell that the new stopover improves (orange). The blue row and column belong to the stopover being added. After the fifth step the table is final.
figures.alt: Six five by five tables of travel minutes. The first holds only the direct rides, with infinity where there is no direct ride. Each next table allows one more stopover, in the order Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev, Eli, and highlights cells that got smaller. The last table has no infinity left and every entry is a shortest travel time.

figures.caption: Johnson's reweighting. Each person gets a score (the cheapest way to reach them from a helper tied to everyone at cost 0). Adding the starting score and subtracting the ending score to each cost removes the negative cost, and every route between the same two people shifts by the same amount.
figures.alt: Two copies of a four-person directed network. On the left the tie from Ben to Cleo costs minus 2 and is drawn in red. On the right every cost has been adjusted using scores of 0, 0, minus 2 and 0 for Ana, Ben, Cleo and Dev, so all costs are zero or more.

figures.caption: Rough counts of basic steps (not seconds) to fill the whole table. Floyd-Warshall pays for every triple of people no matter how few ties there are. Repeated search and Johnson pay in proportion to the ties.
figures.alt: Four groups of three horizontal bars on a log scale, one group per network size. In every group the Floyd-Warshall bar is longest. For the sparse networks the other two bars are two to three powers of ten shorter. For the 1,000 person network with 100,000 ties the three bars are closer together.

figures.caption: Memory for a full distance table at 4 bytes per entry. Ten times more people means a hundred times more table, which is why very large networks answer distance questions without ever writing the whole table down.
figures.alt: Four horizontal bars on a log scale. Each is a hundred times longer than the one above: 4 megabytes for a thousand people, 400 megabytes for ten thousand, 40 gigabytes for a hundred thousand and 4 terabytes for a million. The last two are drawn in red.

figures.caption: Eccentricity is a person's distance to whoever is farthest from them. The people with the smallest value (radius 2) form the center; those with the largest (diameter 4) sit on the edge.
figures.alt: On the left, the ten-person network. Hana, with eccentricity 2, is the one green square. Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev, Eli and Jo, with eccentricity 4, are orange circles; Fay, Gus and Ivo, at 3, are blue circles. On the right, ten horizontal bars sorted by eccentricity.

figures.caption: A network in two pieces. Averaging only the pairs that can reach each other gives a small, friendly number and hides that 18 of the 30 ordered pairs cannot reach each other at all. Report how many pairs are cut off, or use a measure that counts them.
figures.alt: Two groups of three people each, tied within the group and not between groups. Beside them, a six by six table of distances: the two three by three blocks along the diagonal hold 0, 1 and 2, and the rest is infinity, shaded orange. Below, two averages: 1.17 over reachable pairs, and 0.37 when unreachable pairs count as zero efficiency.

figures.caption: Counting shortest routes. One breadth-first search from the top left also counts: each person's number is the sum of the numbers of the neighbors one step closer. The far corner has 10 shortest routes.
figures.alt: A grid of twelve people in three rows and four columns. The top-left dot is 1. The first row reads 1, 1, 1, 1, the second 1, 2, 3, 4 and the third 1, 3, 6, 10. Darker shading marks people farther from the start. The bottom-right dot shows 10.

figures.caption: Number of shortest routes from Jo to each person. Orange ties are the ones on some shortest route. Only Dev has two shortest routes from Jo (one through Fay, one through Gus); everyone else has exactly one.
figures.alt: The ten-person network with each dot showing a count from Jo. Jo shows 1, Ivo 1, Hana 1, Fay 1, Gus 1, then Ana 1, Ben 1, Cleo 1, Dev 2 and Eli 1. Ties that lie on a shortest route from Jo are orange and thick; the others are thin and gray.

figures.caption: Backtracking. From Ana the search tries each neighbor, then that person's neighbors, never stepping on someone already on the route. Green leaves are routes to Eli (4 of them); gray leaves are dead ends where the search backs up.
figures.alt: On the left, a network of Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev and Eli. On the right, a tree that starts at Ana and branches into every route the search tries. Four branches end at Eli and are drawn green. Other branches end at someone who has no unvisited neighbor and are drawn gray.

figures.caption: The first four routes from Ana to Gus, shortest first. Three tie at 2 steps (through Ben, Dev or Fay); the fourth takes 3. 48 routes exist in all that never repeat a person.
figures.alt: Four copies of the ten-person network. In each, one route from Ana to Gus is drawn thickly. The first three routes have 2 steps and go through Ben, through Dev and through Fay. The fourth route has 3 steps.

figures.caption: Counting walks is easy (multiply the tie table by itself) and the answer keeps growing. Counting routes that never repeat a person is a different question, and for Ana to Eli it stays at 4.
figures.alt: A bar chart on a log scale of the number of walks from Ana to Eli of each length from 1 to 10. There are none for lengths 1 and 2, then 2, 2, and so on, growing steadily to 1160. A dashed blue line at 4 marks the routes that never repeat anyone.

figures.caption: Routes between opposite corners of a 4 by 4 grid, by length. There are 20 shortest routes (6 steps) and 184 in all. Most routes are long and winding.
figures.alt: A bar chart with one bar for each route length from 6 to 14 steps. The first bar, in blue, is 20. The bars grow to a peak and shrink again. The bars add up to 184.

figures.caption: Routes between opposite corners of a square grid of people. Shortest routes grow steadily (252 on a 6 by 6 grid). Routes that never repeat a person grow wildly: 1,262,816 on a 6 by 6 grid, and each extra person per side multiplies the count by more than the last.
figures.alt: A line chart on a log scale. The blue line for shortest routes climbs from 2 on a 2 by 2 grid to 924 on a 7 by 7 grid. The red dashed line for all routes that never repeat a person climbs much faster: 2, 12, 184, 8,512, then 1,262,816 for the 6 by 6 grid, where it stops. A table at the right lists the same numbers.

figures.caption: Capping the work honestly. A listing that stops at a limit must say it stopped and report its result as a lower bound. On this 6 by 6 grid the true count is 1,262,816, over a hundred times the limit.
figures.alt: Two cards. The left one, green, reports a limit of 10,000 routes, 10,000 listed, stopped by the limit, so at least 10,000. The right one, red and dashed, reports 10,000 routes found and says nothing about the limit, leaving the reader to think that is the total, when the true total is 1,262,816.
